title: Compactness
objectives: Prove that closed bounded intervals are compact and that continuous functions on compact sets are bounded.

screens.title: Where can a sequence settle
screens.prose: Each picture shows a set and a sequence in it. Flip through them. For each set, ask: does every sequence in it have a subsequence converging inside the set?

state.caption: A: $[0, 1]$, with a sequence that bounces from side to side.

frames.caption: A: $[0, 1]$, with a sequence that bounces from side to side.
C: $[0, \infty)$, with $x_n = n$ running off to the right.

screens.question: Select all that apply: in which sets does every sequence have a subsequence converging to a point of the set?

options.why: $\tfrac1n$ and all its subsequences tend to 0, which is not in $(0, 1]$.
$x_n = n$ has no convergent subsequence: every subsequence is unbounded.

hints.text: Look for a sequence whose subsequences all escape.
In B the limit 0 is missing; in C the terms run off.
In D the limit 0 is included, and in A Bolzano-Weierstrass applies.

feedback.correct: Right. A and D trap their sequences; B loses the limit and C lets it run away.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. In each set, try $\tfrac1n$ and $n$, and check whether the limit belongs to the set.

byKey.B: You accepted $(0, 1]$. Its sequence $\tfrac1n$ settles at 0, outside it.
byKey.C: You accepted $[0, \infty)$. The sequence $n$ settles nowhere.

explain.text: In $[0, 1]$ any sequence has a convergent subsequence (l9), and its limit stays in $[0, 1]$. D keeps the only possible limit point, 0. B misses its limit and C is unbounded.

screens.title: Compact sets
screens.prose: A subset $K$ of a metric space is **compact** (sequentially compact) when this always works. Every sequence in $K$ has a subsequence converging to a point of $K$. Two things can go wrong: the terms run away, or the limit falls outside $K$.
screens.question: Which failure does $(0, 1]$ show?

options.text: The limit falls outside: $\tfrac1n$ and its subsequences tend to $0 \notin (0, 1]$.
The terms run away to infinity.
options.why: $(0, 1]$ is bounded: every term lies between 0 and 1.
The sequence $\tfrac1n$ has no subsequence converging inside $(0, 1]$.

options.text: The terms oscillate, so nothing converges.
options.why: $\tfrac1n$ does not oscillate; it converges, only to the wrong place.

hints.text: Is $(0, 1]$ bounded?
Yes. So look at where limits land.
$\tfrac1n \to 0$, and 0 is missing.

feedback.correct: Right. Bounded, but the limit escapes.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Is $(0, 1]$ bounded, and is it closed?

explain.text: Every subsequence of $\tfrac1n$ tends to 0, which is not in $(0, 1]$. So $(0, 1]$ is not compact, though bounded. The missing ingredient is closedness (l23).

screens.title: Step 1: a convergent subsequence
screens.prose: We prove that $[a, b]$ is compact. Let $(x_n)$ be any sequence with $a \le x_n \le b$ for all $n$.
screens.question: Why does some subsequence $x_{n_k}$ converge?

options.text: $(x_n)$ is bounded, so Bolzano-Weierstrass (l9) gives a convergent subsequence.

options.why: Nothing makes $(x_n)$ monotone. Sequence A bounced from side to side.
A bounded sequence need not be Cauchy: $0, 1, 0, 1, \dots$ lies in $[0, 1]$.

options.text: $(x_n)$ itself converges, since it is trapped in $[a, b]$.
options.why: Trapped is not convergent: $0, 1, 0, 1, \dots$ stays in $[0, 1]$ and diverges.

hints.text: What do we know about $(x_n)$? Only that $a \le x_n \le b$.
So $(x_n)$ is bounded.
Bounded sequences have convergent subsequences.

feedback.correct: Right. Bounded gives a convergent subsequence.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use only the bound $a \le x_n \le b$.

explain.text: All we know is $a \le x_n \le b$, so $(x_n)$ is bounded. Bolzano-Weierstrass then gives $x_{n_k} \to x$ for some real $x$. Where $x$ lies is the next step.

screens.title: Step 2: the limit stays inside
screens.prose: So $x_{n_k} \to x$ for some real $x$. To finish we need $x \in [a, b]$.
screens.question: Why is $x \in [a, b]$?

options.text: $[a, b]$ is closed, and closed sets contain the limits of their convergent sequences (l23).
Bolzano-Weierstrass puts the limit in $[a, b]$.
options.why: It promises a limit, not where it lies. On $(0, 1]$ the limit 0 escapes.
$(0, 1]$ is bounded too, and its limits can escape. Closedness is what keeps them.

options.text: Each term is in $[a, b]$, so the limit is, for any set.
options.why: Not for any set: $\tfrac1n \in (0, 1]$ tends to $0 \notin (0, 1]$.

hints.text: Which property of $[a, b]$ fails for $(0, 1]$?
$[a, b]$ includes its ends: it is closed.
Closed sets keep limits of their sequences.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the property that $[a, b]$ has and $(0, 1]$ lacks.

explain.text: $a \le x_{n_k} \le b$ and limits keep $\le$, so $a \le x \le b$. That is the l23 theorem for the closed set $[a, b]$. Bounded gave the limit; closed kept it.

screens.title: Closed intervals are compact
screens.prose: Assemble the proof that $[a, b]$ is compact. One line is flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: Let $(x_n)$ be a sequence in $[a, b]$.
It is bounded, so by Bolzano-Weierstrass some subsequence $x_{n_k}$ converges, to $x$ say.
$[a, b]$ is closed, so it contains the limit: $x \in [a, b]$.
So every sequence in $[a, b]$ has a subsequence converging in $[a, b]$: it is compact. $\blacksquare$
Since $(x_n)$ is bounded, $(x_n)$ converges to some $x$.
lines.why: Bounded sequences need not converge: $0, 1, 0, 1, \dots$ Only a subsequence is promised.

hints.text: Start with an arbitrary sequence.
Bounded gives a convergent subsequence.
Closed keeps its limit.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take a sequence, extract a subsequence, then place its limit.

byKey.d1: You let the whole sequence converge. Only a subsequence does.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the flawed line goes to Left out.

explain.text: Bounded and closed each do one job. The same two steps prove any closed, bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}$ compact. That is half of the Heine-Borel theorem.

screens.title: The Heine-Borel theorem
screens.prose: **Heine-Borel** in $\mathbb{R}$: $K$ is compact exactly when it is closed and bounded. The last screen proved one direction. For the other, compact implies closed by l23's sequence test, and compact implies bounded.

state.caption: C: $[0, \infty)$, with $x_n = n$ running off to the right.

screens.question: Why is a compact $K$ bounded?

options.text: If not, pick $x_n \in K$ with $|x_n| > n$; no subsequence converges, since convergent sequences are bounded.
Compact sets are closed, and closed sets are bounded.
options.why: $[0, \infty)$ is closed and unbounded.

options.text: A compact set is finite, so it is bounded.
options.why: $[0, 1]$ is compact and infinite.
Bolzano-Weierstrass needs a bounded sequence to start. Here boundedness is what we want to prove.

hints.text: Argue by contradiction: suppose $K$ is unbounded.
Then for each $n$ some $x_n \in K$ has $|x_n| > n$.
A convergent subsequence would be bounded, but $|x_{n_k}| > n_k \ge k$.

feedback.correct: Right. An unbounded $K$ holds a sequence that runs away, like $n$ in $[0, \infty)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Suppose $K$ is unbounded and build a sequence that escapes.

explain.text: If $K$ is unbounded, pick $x_n \in K$ with $|x_n| > n$. Any subsequence has $|x_{n_k}| > k$, so it is unbounded and cannot converge. So compact sets in $\mathbb{R}$ are closed and bounded, and nothing more is needed.

screens.title: Extremes on any compact set
screens.prose: The proof of l17 works on any compact $K$ in a metric space. Prove: a continuous $f: K \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded above and attains its supremum. One line is flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: Suppose $f$ is unbounded above: pick $x_n \in K$ with $f(x_n) > n$.
Compactness gives $x_{n_k} \to c \in K$, so $f(x_{n_k}) \to f(c)$ by continuity; yet $f(x_{n_k}) > k$. So $f$ is bounded above; let $M = \sup f(K)$.
For each $n$ pick $y_n \in K$ with $f(y_n) > M - \tfrac1n$.
By continuity $f(y_{n_k}) \to f(d)$, and $M - \tfrac1{n_k} < f(y_{n_k}) \le M$ squeezes $f(d) = M$. $\blacksquare$
$K$ is bounded, so Bolzano-Weierstrass gives a convergent subsequence of $(x_n)$.
lines.why: In a general metric space, bounded gives no subsequence. Compactness itself supplies one, with its limit in $K$.

hints.text: First rule out unboundedness by contradiction.
Then take points whose values approach the supremum $M$.
Each time, compactness gives a subsequence with its limit in $K$.

feedback.correct: Right. Compactness does the work of Bolzano-Weierstrass and closedness together.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Bounded first, then a sequence approaching $M$, then the squeeze.

byKey.d1: You used Bolzano-Weierstrass. That is a fact about $\mathbb{R}$; in a metric space compactness is what gives the subsequence.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the flawed line goes to Left out.

explain.text: In l17, Bolzano-Weierstrass found the subsequence and closedness kept its limit in $[a, b]$. Compactness packages both. So the theorem holds on any compact set, such as a closed bounded set in $\mathbb{R}^n$.

screens.title: Uniform continuity, again
screens.prose: In l20 we proved that continuous on $[a, b]$ implies uniformly continuous. That proof took $x_n, y_n$ with $d(x_n, y_n) < \tfrac1n$ and $|f(x_n) - f(y_n)| \ge \varepsilon_0$, then found $x_{n_k} \to c$ with $c \in [a, b]$.

state.caption: Not uniformly continuous: near 0 the curve is too steep for one $\delta$.

screens.question: On a compact $K$, what replaces that step?

options.text: Compactness of $K$ gives $x_{n_k} \to c \in K$ directly; the rest of the proof is unchanged.

options.why: Bolzano-Weierstrass is about $\mathbb{R}$. On a general $K$, compactness is the replacement.
Closed alone gives no convergent subsequence: $[0, \infty)$ is closed and $x_n = n$ escapes.

options.text: Nothing: the result needs $K$ to be an interval.
options.why: The proof used only a convergent subsequence with its limit in the set. Compactness gives exactly that.

hints.text: Which two facts about $[a, b]$ did the step use?
A convergent subsequence, and its limit inside the set.
Compactness of $K$ gives both at once.

feedback.correct: Right. Continuous on compact implies uniformly continuous.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the old step needed, and what supplies it on $K$.

explain.text: The step needed a subsequence converging to a point of the set. Compactness gives that on any $K$. So continuous functions on compact sets are uniformly continuous, as $\tfrac1x$ on $(0, 1]$ shows they may not be otherwise.

screens.title: Covering with open intervals
screens.prose: An **open cover** of a set is a family of open sets whose union contains it. The intervals $(\tfrac1n, 1)$ for $n \ge 2$ cover $(0, 1)$: each $x \in (0, 1)$ lies in one once $\tfrac1n < x$.
screens.question: Do finitely many of them cover $(0, 1)$?

options.text: No: finitely many have a largest $n$, say $N$, and they miss $(0, \tfrac1N]$.
Yes, a large enough $n$ alone covers it.
options.why: $(\tfrac1n, 1)$ misses $\tfrac1{2n}$, for every $n$.
Their union is $(\tfrac13, 1)$, which misses 0.1.
$[0.01, 0.99]$ is infinite too, and one interval covers it (next screen). The gap near 0 is what matters.

hints.text: Finitely many intervals have a largest $n$.
Their union is $(\tfrac1N, 1)$.
That misses $\tfrac1{2N} \in (0, 1)$.

feedback.correct: Right. No finite subcover: the gap near 0 never closes.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the union of finitely many of these intervals.

explain.text: Finitely many intervals have union $(\tfrac1N, 1)$ for their largest $N$. It misses $\tfrac1{2N}$. In $\mathbb{R}$, a set is compact exactly when every open cover has a finite subcover, and $(0, 1)$ fails.

screens.title: A closed piece needs one interval
screens.prose: Now cover the closed interval $[0.01, 0.99]$ with the same family $(\tfrac1n, 1)$.
screens.question: What is the smallest $n$ with $[0.01, 0.99] \subseteq (\tfrac1n, 1)$?

hints.text: We need $\tfrac1n < 0.01$.
$\tfrac1{100} = 0.01$ is not below 0.01, and the interval is open.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $\tfrac1n < 0.01$ for the smallest whole $n$.

byKey.equal: $(\tfrac1{100}, 1) = (0.01, 1)$ leaves out 0.01 itself, which is in the set.

explain.text: $\tfrac1n < 0.01$ needs $n > 100$, so $n = 101$, since $\tfrac1{101} \approx 0.0099$. One interval covers $[0.01, 0.99]$. A closed, bounded set leaves no gap for the cover to chase.

screens.title: Half the conditions
screens.prose: Heine-Borel needs both closed and bounded. A common slip is to check one and stop.
screens.question: Select all that apply: which subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ are compact?

options.why: You checked bounded and stopped. $1 - \tfrac1n$ tends to $1 \notin (0, 1)$.
You checked closed and stopped. $x_n = n$ has no convergent subsequence.
Closed, but unbounded: $x_n = n$ escapes.
Bounded, but not closed: rationals can tend to $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2} \notin \mathbb{Q}$.

hints.text: Test each set for closed and for bounded.
$(0, 1)$ and $[0, 1] \cap \mathbb{Q}$ are bounded but not closed.
$[0, \infty)$ and $\mathbb{Z}$ are closed but not bounded.

feedback.correct: Right. Only the closed and bounded sets.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check both conditions for every set.

byKey.open: Bounded, so compact? $(0, 1)$ loses the limit 1.
byKey.ray: Closed, so compact? $[0, \infty)$ lets $n$ run away.
byKey.Q: Bounded, so compact? Its limits can be irrational.

explain.text: $[-2, 2] \cup \{5\}$ and $\{1, 2, 3\}$ are closed and bounded, so compact. Each other set has one condition and lacks the other. 'Bounded, so compact' and 'closed, so compact' are both wrong.

screens.title: When an optimiser has an answer
screens.prose: Two assets return 5% and 8% a year. The weights $w = (w_1, w_2)$ have $w_1 + w_2 = 1$. On long-only weights ($w_i \ge 0$) the expected return $0.05w_1 + 0.08w_2$ is continuous on a closed, bounded set. Now require every weight strictly positive.

state.caption: Strictly positive weights: $0 < w_2 < 1$, ends left out.

screens.question: On strictly positive weights, what is the supremum of the expected return?

hints.text: The return $0.05 + 0.03w_2$ rises with $w_2$.
$w_2$ can approach 1 but not equal it.
So the supremum is $0.05 + 0.03 = 8\%$.

feedback.correct: Right. 8% is the supremum, but no strictly positive portfolio attains it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Push $w_2$ towards 1 and see what the return approaches.

byKey.mid: 6.5% is the equal-weight return. The return keeps rising as $w_2$ grows.

explain.text: The supremum is 8%, but every strictly positive portfolio earns less, so there is no optimum. On the closed, bounded long-only set the maximum 8% is attained at $w = (0, 1)$. With a continuous objective, compactness guarantees a long-only optimum, while a strict constraint can leave none.

ideas: Compact: every sequence in $K$ has a subsequence converging to a point of $K$. $[0, 1]$ and $\{\tfrac1n\} \cup \{0\}$ are; $(0, 1]$ and $[0, \infty)$ are not.
$[a, b]$ is compact: Bolzano-Weierstrass gives the subsequence and closedness keeps its limit. Heine-Borel: in $\mathbb{R}$, compact means closed and bounded.
On a compact set a continuous function is bounded, attains its extremes and is uniformly continuous. $(\tfrac1n, 1)$ covers $(0, 1)$ with no finite subcover.

formula.name: Heine-Borel on the real line
formula.tex: K \text{ compact} \iff K \text{ closed and bounded}
formula.note: In a general metric space it fails: $\mathbb{N}$ with the discrete metric is closed and bounded, not compact.

summary.trap: 'Bounded, so compact' fails for $(0, 1)$, and 'closed, so compact' fails for $[0, \infty)$.

quiz.prose: Give $\mathbb{N}$ the discrete metric: $d(m, n) = 1$ for $m \ne n$. Then $\mathbb{N}$ is closed in itself and bounded, since every distance is at most 1.
quiz.question: Is $\mathbb{N}$ compact in this metric?

options.text: No: $1, 2, 3, \dots$ has no convergent subsequence, since its terms are all distance 1 apart.
Yes, by Heine-Borel: it is closed and bounded.
options.why: Heine-Borel is a theorem about $\mathbb{R}$ (and $\mathbb{R}^n$). In a general metric space it can fail, as here.

options.text: Yes, since every ball of radius 2 is finite.
options.why: The ball of radius 2 is all of $\mathbb{N}$, which is infinite.
In this metric every distance is at most 1, so it is bounded.

feedback.correct: Right. Closed and bounded is not enough in a general metric space.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which subsequences of $1, 2, 3, \dots$ converge in the discrete metric?

explain.text: In the discrete metric only eventually constant sequences converge (l22). A subsequence of $1, 2, 3, \dots$ has distinct terms, so none converges. Heine-Borel uses the structure of $\mathbb{R}$, not just closed and bounded.

quiz.prose: Let $K$ be any finite subset of a metric space.
quiz.question: Why is $K$ compact?

options.text: Some point of $K$ appears infinitely often in any sequence, giving a constant subsequence.

options.why: That argument works only in $\mathbb{R}^n$. The finite case needs no Heine-Borel.
A sequence may repeat points: $a, b, a, b, \dots$ lies in $\{a, b\}$.
Bolzano-Weierstrass is about $\mathbb{R}$; here we may be in any metric space.

feedback.correct: Right. Pigeonholes give a constant subsequence.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Infinitely many terms, finitely many points: what must happen?

explain.text: Infinitely many terms land on finitely many points, so one point $p$ is hit infinitely often. Those terms form a constant subsequence, which converges to $p \in K$. So every finite set is compact.

quiz.question: What is the smallest $n$ for which one interval suffices?

byKey.two: $(\tfrac12, 1)$ misses almost all of the set.

explain.text: We need $\tfrac1n < 0.001$, so $n > 1000$ and $n = 1001$. The right end 0.5 is inside $(\tfrac1n, 1)$ already. A compact set needs only finitely many, here one.

quiz.prose: $f(x) = x^2$ is continuous on the compact set $[-1, 2]$.
quiz.question: What is its maximum value?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the values at the end points and at the flat point 0.

byKey.left: 1 is the value at $-1$. The end point 2 gives more.

explain.text: The candidates are $f(-1) = 1$, $f(0) = 0$ and $f(2) = 4$. The maximum is 4 at $x = 2$ and the minimum 0 at $x = 0$. Compactness guarantees both exist.
